summary: The rate at which velocity changes, measured in metres per second squared.
detail: a = Δv / t for constant acceleration. Because velocity has direction, turning at steady speed is also accelerating.

summary: Speed together with direction; the rate of change of position.
detail: Average velocity is displacement over time. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so a car on a roundabout at constant speed still has changing velocity.

summary: Any interaction that changes an object's motion or shape; F = ma.
detail: One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s². Forces always come in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's third law).

summary: The SI unit of force: the force needed to accelerate one kilogram at one metre per second squared.
The amount of matter in an object — a measure of its inertia, unchanged by location.
detail: Mass is not weight: a 70 kg astronaut has the same mass on the Moon but only about one sixth of the weight.

summary: The force of gravity on an object: W = mg.
detail: On Earth g is about 9.80665 m/s², so a 1 kg mass weighs about 9.81 N. Weight changes with location; mass does not.

summary: The acceleration caused by gravitational attraction; at the Earth's surface about 9.80665 m/s².
detail: g varies slightly with latitude and altitude — about 9.78 m/s² at the equator and 9.83 m/s² at the poles.

summary: The SI unit of energy and work: one newton-metre, or one watt for one second.
detail: Lifting an apple about one metre takes roughly one joule. A kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules.

summary: Energy transferred by a force moving an object: W = Fd cos θ.
detail: Pushing a wall does no work in the physics sense — the wall does not move, so no energy is transferred.

summary: The energy an object has because it is moving: ½mv².
detail: Because velocity is squared, doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy — which is why stopping distances grow fourfold when speed doubles.

summary: Energy stored because of position: mgh near the Earth's surface, ½kx² in a spring.
The rate of energy transfer: one watt is one joule per second.
detail: P = W/t, and electrically P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

summary: Mass times velocity; the quantity conserved when no external force acts.
detail: Momentum has direction. In a rocket or a collision, total momentum before and after is the same (Newton's third law in action).

summary: Mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V.
detail: Water is about 1000 kg/m³, air at sea level about 1.2 kg/m³, steel about 7850 kg/m³. Objects float when their density is lower than the fluid's.

summary: Force per unit area: one pascal is one newton per square metre.
detail: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 101 325 Pa. Pressure acts in all directions, which is why a dam wall is built thicker at the bottom.

summary: The capacity to do work, measured in joules; it is conserved, only converted between forms.
detail: Falling water converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, and a turbine converts that into electrical energy — each step losing some to heat.

summary: For a wave, speed = frequency × wavelength: v = fλ.
detail: Light in vacuum always travels at c = 299 792 458 m/s regardless of wavelength; in a medium its speed drops by the refractive index factor.

summary: How many cycles happen per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
detail: Period T = 1/f. A 50 Hz mains supply completes 50 cycles every second, so its period is 20 ms.

summary: Voltage equals current times resistance: V = IR.
detail: It holds for ohmic conductors at constant temperature. Combining with P = VI gives P = I²R and P = V²/R.

summary: The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts.
detail: One volt is one joule per coulomb. Voltage is always measured *between* two points.

summary: The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).
detail: Conventional current flows from positive to negative, the opposite direction to the electrons themselves.

summary: How strongly a component opposes current: R = V/I.
Charge stored per volt across a capacitor: C = Q/V.
detail: Energy stored is ½CV². In an RC circuit the time constant τ = RC is the time to reach about 63% of the final voltage.

summary: PV = nRT links pressure, volume, amount of gas and temperature.
detail: Holds well for gases at low pressure. R = 8.314462618… J/(mol·K).

summary: 299 792 458 m/s in vacuum, exactly, by definition of the metre.
detail: Nothing carrying information can exceed it. It takes light about 1.28 s to travel from the Moon to the Earth.

summary: The constant in Newton's law of gravitation, about 6.6743 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².
Light bends at a boundary so that n₁sin θ₁ = n₂sin θ₂.
detail: The refractive index n = c/v measures how much a medium slows light. Going from dense to thin glass at a steep angle gives total internal reflection — the basis of fibre optics.

summary: The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.
detail: After n half-lives the fraction remaining is (1/2)^n, so after 10 half-lives less than 0.1% is left. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years.

summary: The energy needed to raise one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin.
detail: Water needs 4186 J/(kg·K) — unusually high, which is why it is used in heating systems and why coastal climates are mild.

summary: Useful output energy divided by total input energy, usually given as a percentage.
detail: Real machines are always below 100% because of friction, heat loss and sound. A car engine is typically 25–40% efficient.

summary: Motion under gravity alone, with no air resistance.
detail: All objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass (g ≈ 9.81 m/s²). Feather and hammer dropped on the Moon land together, as Apollo 15 showed.

summary: The point where an object's mass can be treated as concentrated for many calculations.
detail: An object balances on its centre of mass. For a uniform rod it is the midpoint; for a triangle it is the average of the three vertices.

summary: The extension of a spring is proportional to the force applied: F = kx, up to the elastic limit.
detail: The energy stored in a stretched spring is ½kx², not kx — the force rises as the spring stretches.

summary: The change in observed frequency when a source and observer move relative to each other.
detail: An approaching siren sounds higher, a receding one lower. The same effect on light gives the redshift used to measure how fast galaxies recede.

summary: A measure of how many ways a system's energy can be arranged — of its disorder.
detail: The second law of thermodynamics says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases: heat flows hot to cold, and perpetual motion machines are impossible.

summary: The turning effect of a force: τ = F·d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
detail: Torque is what tightens a bolt: the same force on a longer spanner turns it more easily.

summary: Force multiplied by the time it acts: it equals the change in momentum.
detail: Airbags and crumple zones stretch the impact time so the same momentum change needs a smaller force.

summary: The distance between two identical points on a wave, such as crest to crest.
detail: Visible light runs from about 380 nm (violet) to 750 nm (red).

summary: A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance, in kelvin, celsius or fahrenheit.
detail: Absolute zero (0 K = −273.15 °C) is the point at which no more thermal energy can be removed. Kelvin is the SI unit and has no degree symbol.

summary: Energy transferred because of a temperature difference, measured in joules.
detail: Heat and temperature are different: a bath of warm water holds more heat than a red-hot nail, even though the nail is hotter.

summary: How much a medium slows light: n = c/v.
detail: Water is about 1.33, window glass 1.5, diamond 2.42 — which is why diamonds sparkle so strongly.

summary: The region where magnetic forces act, measured in tesla.
detail: The Earth's field is about 50 microtesla; an MRI scanner is 1.5–3 tesla, tens of thousands of times stronger.

summary: Force per unit positive charge at a point, measured in volts per metre.
The SI base unit of temperature, starting at absolute zero with no negative values.
detail: K = °C + 273.15. A change of one kelvin equals a change of one degree celsius.

summary: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.
detail: It links forces to motion without needing to track time, and explains why braking distance grows with the square of speed.
